lessons.title: Health and nuisance pests and their risks
lessons.html:
Why these pests matter

Health pests transmit disease or contaminate food; nuisance pests cause discomfort, damage or distress. Both are major concerns in homes, food premises, farms, hospitals, schools and silo complexes. Food premises in South Africa are required under the food hygiene regulations made under the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 to be kept free of pests, and municipal environmental health practitioners inspect them.

Main groups

PestKey risks
Rats and miceContaminate food with droppings and urine; diseases such as leptospirosis and salmonellosis; gnaw cables causing fires; fleas from rodents can transmit plague
Cockroaches (German, American)Carry bacteria onto food surfaces; trigger allergies and asthma
FliesBreed in waste and manure; carry pathogens to food
MosquitoesMalaria in parts of Limpopo, Mpumalanga and northern KwaZulu-Natal; nuisance biting elsewhere
Fleas, bed bugs, ticks, liceBites, irritation, some disease transmission, distress
AntsFood contamination; some sting
Pest birds such as feral pigeonsDroppings foul product and structures and may carry pathogens; nests block gutters

Biology that guides control

  • Norway rats burrow and live at ground level; roof rats climb and nest high in roofs and trees; house mice explore small territories and enter gaps about the width of a pencil.
  • German cockroaches live indoors in warm, humid harbourages near food, such as motors and kitchen equipment, and breed rapidly. American cockroaches are larger and often live in drains and sewers.
  • House flies can complete development in about a week or two in warm weather, so breeding sites must be removed promptly.
  • Mosquitoes breed in standing water, including blocked gutters, old tyres and containers.
  • Bed bugs hide in mattress seams, bed frames and furniture near sleeping people, and spread through luggage and second-hand furniture.

lessons.title: Control strategies for rodents and insects
lessons.html:
Rodent management

  1. Inspect for droppings, runways, burrows and entry points.
  2. Sanitation: remove spillage and accessible food, store food in rodent-proof containers, manage refuse.
  3. Proofing: seal gaps around pipes, doors and vents with durable materials such as steel mesh, concrete and door strips.
  4. Trapping: snap traps or multi-catch traps in sensitive areas such as food production, where poison is not appropriate.
  5. Baiting: registered rodenticides in tamper-resistant, secured, labelled bait stations, placed along runways outside or in permitted areas.
  6. Monitoring: numbered stations on a site plan, checked at each service.

Most rodenticides are anticoagulants. Second-generation anticoagulants are potent and persistent and pose a risk of secondary poisoning to owls, raptors, dogs and cats. Use them strictly according to the label, search for and dispose of carcasses, and remove bait at the end of a treatment where the label requires. In suspected human or pet poisoning, get medical or veterinary help immediately and take the label; a doctor or vet decides on treatment.

Cockroaches

  • Improve sanitation and remove clutter and harbourage.
  • Use gel baits placed precisely in cracks and crevices near harbourage.
  • Use insect growth regulators where registered to break the breeding cycle.
  • Avoid spraying repellent products over baits.
  • Monitor with sticky traps to find hot spots and measure results.

Flies and mosquitoes

  • Remove breeding sites: manage refuse, manure and drainage, empty or cover standing water.
  • Use screens, air curtains and strip curtains on food premises.
  • Use insect light traps with catch trays in food areas rather than devices that scatter insect fragments.
  • Apply registered larvicides or adulticides where justified.

Bed bugs and fleas

Thorough inspection, laundering on hot cycles, vacuuming, encasements and targeted registered treatments, with follow-up visits because eggs may survive. For fleas, pets must be treated by the owner with veterinary products at the same time as the premises.

Pest birds

Use proofing such as netting, spikes and wires, remove nesting material and food sources. Some birds are protected; check provincial conservation requirements before any lethal control.

lessons.title: Working safely in sensitive environments
lessons.html:
Sensitive sites

Health and nuisance pest work often takes place where people are most vulnerable or where contamination risk is highest: kitchens, food factories, hospitals, crèches, old age homes and homes with children and pets.

Food premises

  • Do not apply products onto food or food contact surfaces; remove or cover food and utensils.
  • Treat outside production times where possible, and allow the label re-entry period before production resumes.
  • Use non-chemical methods and baits rather than sprays in production areas.
  • Never place loose rodenticide in food production or storage areas; use traps or secured stations as permitted by the label and the client's food safety system.
  • Provide the client with documentation for audits: site plan, service reports, trend analysis, product labels and SDSs, and operator registration.

Homes, schools and health facilities

  • Ask about occupants with asthma, allergies or pregnancy, and about pets, fish and birds.
  • Choose low-risk formulations and targeted placement.
  • Explain preparation and re-entry clearly and give written instructions.
  • Keep bait stations secured and out of reach.

Personal safety

  • Wear PPE specified on the label and gloves when handling rodent carcasses, droppings and nests. Avoid stirring up dust from droppings; wet the area with disinfectant before cleaning as your procedure requires.
  • Wash hands thoroughly after each job.
  • Be alert to needles, sharp objects and biohazards in drains, roof spaces and refuse areas.
  • Take care on ladders and in roof spaces.

Evaluating results

Health pest programmes are judged by measurable outcomes: zero rodent activity in production areas, declining insect light trap counts, no live cockroaches on sticky monitors, no customer complaints. Review trends with the client and agree corrective actions, especially where hygiene or proofing issues are the client's responsibility.

Key points

  • Food premises must be kept free of pests and are inspected by environmental health practitioners.
  • Rodents spread diseases such as leptospirosis; cockroaches and flies carry pathogens to food.
  • Base control on sanitation, proofing, monitoring and targeted baits rather than general spraying.
  • Use rodenticides only in secured stations as labelled, and manage secondary poisoning risk.
  • In food areas never contaminate food or food contact surfaces, and keep audit documentation complete.
